title: Cap. XII: Blancus — death in Adam multiplied; Rom 5:15 offense and justice
pass_a_gloss: What he also adds—'inasmuch as in him they died'—confirms our view: for when all are said to die in Adam, Adam's own death is not understood as one in number, imputed to all; but death multiplied according to the number of men, and each one's own. He adds, and they died by the offense of that one man (Rom. 5:15); whence, he says, it is ready to gather that that offense was everyone's offense, namely by imputation: for it is contrary to divine justice that anyone should share another's punishment and not share the guilt in any way. If someone likewise said we were produced by that one man's operation or power, would it follow that that operation or power was common to all by imputation? If it is contrary to divine justice that anyone share another's punishment and not share guilt in any way, certainly it is also contrary to the same justice that one who otherwise would not share guilt should be made a sharer of guilt by the judge's imputation. If a judge acts unjustly in laying a penalty on one who in no way shares guilt, how much greater the injustice if he not only lays on the penalty but by his own act and judicial imputation also makes him a sharer of guilt—and so a sinner and guilty—who otherwise was neither sinner nor guilty? I marvel that pious and learned men do not consider this. For who that is innocent could not be justly punished, if imputation makes common a sin that otherwise would not have been common, and makes truly a sinner and guilty one who otherwise would not have been a sinner?
pass_b_english: His added words—'inasmuch as in him they died'—confirm our view. When all are said to die in Adam, we do not mean Adam's single death imputed to everyone, but death multiplied by the number of men, each his own. He adds that they died by that one man's offense (Rom. 5:15), and from this thinks it easy to gather that the offense was everyone's by imputation, since divine justice will not let someone share another's punishment without sharing the guilt somehow. If someone likewise said we were produced by that one man's power, would that power therefore be common to all by imputation? If justice forbids sharing another's punishment without sharing guilt, it also forbids making someone a sharer of guilt by the judge's imputation who otherwise would not share it. If a judge already acts unjustly in punishing one who shares no guilt, how much worse if by his own act and judicial imputation he also makes that man a guilty sinner who otherwise was neither? I marvel that pious and learned men miss this. Who that is innocent could not be 'justly' punished, if imputation makes common a sin that was not common, and makes a true sinner of one who otherwise was not?
source_text: Quod etiam subiungit, quippe in quo mortui sunt, confirmat nostram sententiam: non enim cum in Adamo mori omnes dicuntur, mors ipsius Adami intelligitur, una numero, omnibus imputata; sed mors secundum hominum numerum multiplicata, ac sua cuique propria. Addit, & mortui unius illius hominis offensa Rom. 5. 15. unde, inquit, promptum est colligere, illam offensam fuisse omnium offensam, puta imputatione: repugnat enim justitiae divinae ut quis alienae poenae sit particeps, & non sit ullo modo particeps culpae. Si quis similiter diceret, nos fuisse productos unius illius hominis operatione vel virtute, num inde sequeretur, illam operationem vel virtutem fuisse omnium communem imputatione? Si repugnat justitiae divinae, ut quis alienae poenae sit particeps, & non sit ullo modo particeps culpae, certe eidem etiam justitiae repugnat, ut fiat particeps culpae judicis imputatione, is, qui alioqui non esset culpae particeps. Si judex facit injuste ei poenam irrogans, qui nullo modo est particeps culpae, quanto major erit injustitia, si non modo poenam irroget, sed eum faciat etiam sua actione & judiciaria imputatione participem culpae, atque adeo peccatorem & reum, alioqui non peccatorem nec reum? Miror hoc a viris piis & doctis non considerari. Quis enim innocens puniri juste non poterit, si facit imputatio commune esse peccatum quod alioqui non fuisset commune, & esse vere peccatorem & reum, qui alioqui peccator non fuisset?

choices.choice: many deaths, not one imputed death
choices.why: blocks Blancus's in-quo reading toward immediate guilt
exposes injustice of bare judicial imputation
